thesis: Compatibilism survives the consequence argument once the relevant sense of 'could have done otherwise' is made precise.

claims.statement: The consequence argument relies on a transfer principle for powerlessness that is stronger than it looks.
claims.support: Frankfurt (1971) and responses distinguishing ability from alternative possibilities.

claims.statement: An agent can act freely in a deterministic world if the action flows from a will the agent endorses.
claims.support: Analogy to reasons-responsive capacities that operate the same way whether or not determinism holds.

objections.statement: If every action is fixed by the past and the laws, endorsing one's will is itself fixed, so it cannot ground freedom.
objections.reply: The objection assumes freedom requires an undetermined source; it needs an independent argument that endorsement must be uncaused to count, which it does not supply.

concessions: Whether ordinary agents have the reflective capacities the view requires remains an open empirical question.
engagements: Harry G. Frankfurt, "Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person"
